posts.hook: Your CV says Python. The job asks what you built with it.
posts.body:
Before your next application, match one requirement to one piece of evidence.

Example, fictional: 'Used Python' becomes 'Built a Python script to validate CSV files and flag missing customer IDs.'

The stronger line names the task and the output. Add a result only when you can verify it. Tailoring should make real experience easier to find.
posts.card_title: Make your experience easier to find
points: Find evidence in your real work
Name the task and the output
Keep only claims you can explain

posts.hook: Before sending another application, check these four things.
posts.body:
A role title is only the start of a match.

1. Can you show evidence for the core work?
2. Does the location or remote policy fit?
3. Do you meet the stated work-authorisation requirements?
4. Can you explain why this role fits your next step?

Build a shortlist you can act on. Then tailor the most relevant parts of your CV for each role.
posts.card_title: A shortlist you can act on
points: A clear reason for this role

posts.hook: An autofilled application still needs your judgement.
posts.body:
Before pressing Submit, read the form from top to bottom.

Check the CV version, dates, contact details and portfolio link. Answer salary, notice period, visa and legal questions yourself. Open the attached file once to check it is the version you meant to send.

ApplySarthi helps with the repetitive form filling in your own Chrome. You keep the final review and submission.
points: Your own answers to personal questions

posts.hook: A keyword belongs on your CV only if you can defend it.
posts.body:
Use the job description to identify the language of the role. Then check each term against your own experience.

If you used SQL to investigate a reporting issue, describe that work. If you have never used a tool, do not turn the requirement into a claim.

ApplySarthi can help reword your CV for a role using the experience already in it. Read the result before applying.
points: Describe where you used the skill

posts.hook: The wrong CV attachment can undo careful preparation.
posts.body:
Use a simple final check for every application.

Name the file for the role. Check that your most relevant project is easy to find. Open your portfolio links. Read the uploaded preview when the form offers one.

Keep a record of which version you sent so your interview answers match the experience the employer has read.
points: Name the file for the role

posts.hook: 'I worked on the backend' leaves your interviewer guessing.
posts.body:
Try this structure when you explain a project:

Problem: what needed to change?
Ownership: what did you personally do?
Decision: why did you choose that approach?
Evidence: how did you check it worked?

Example, fictional: 'I wrote the API validation for our booking project. I rejected invalid date ranges before database writes and added tests for overlapping bookings.'

Use your own project. Practise saying it aloud, then explain one trade-off.
points: Evidence: how did you check it?

posts.hook: Your project answer needs a reason for the decision.
posts.body:
'We used Redis' names a tool. The follow-up is often the harder part: why was that a sensible choice for your project?

Practise explaining the constraint, the alternative you considered, and what your choice made harder. If it was a team decision, say so and explain your part.

A useful practice prompt: 'What would make you choose a different approach next time?'
posts.card_title: Explain the decision behind the tool

posts.hook: 'Tell me about yourself' needs a route to this role.
posts.body:
Try a short opening built from three parts.

Now: the work or study you are doing.
Evidence: one relevant project or responsibility.
Next: why that connects to this role.

Skip a complete life history. Record a first attempt and listen for the moment you actually give evidence. Then make that part clearer.

Prep Sarthi gives you a spoken practice conversation based on your own CV.
points: Now: your current work or study
Say it aloud before the interview

posts.hook: For a debugging story, explain the investigation.
posts.body:
A useful answer shows how you narrowed the problem.

What failed? What did you check first? Which evidence ruled out a cause? What changed after the fix?

Example, fictional: 'A report missed some orders. I compared the query results with source records, found a date-boundary condition, changed the filter and added a boundary test.'

Use an incident you actually worked on. Do not add impact numbers you cannot support.

posts.hook: Your team did the project. What was your part?
posts.body:
Use 'we' for the team's goal and 'I' for your contribution.

Example, fictional: 'We built a support dashboard. I wrote the ticket filters and tested the empty-state behaviour. A teammate handled authentication.'

That gives the interviewer a clear place to ask a follow-up. It also keeps your answer honest about what you did and what others owned.

Practise the follow-up: 'What was the hardest decision in your part?'

posts.hook: A gap on your CV needs a clear answer, not an apology.
posts.body:
Prepare a brief, factual explanation at the level of detail you are comfortable sharing. Then connect the conversation to what you can contribute now.

A structure to practise: 'During that period, I [accurate explanation]. Since then, I have [real work, learning or preparation]. I am now looking for [relevant role].'

Keep placeholders as placeholders until you replace them with your own facts.
points: Describe what you can do now
Connect it to the next role

posts.hook: The second interview question is where a memorised answer can break.
posts.body:
After explaining a project, practise one more question:

'Why that approach?'
'What failed the first time?'
'What would change with more users?'
'Which part did you personally own?'

You do not need a script for every possibility. You need to understand your example well enough to discuss it. Prep Sarthi asks follow-ups when an answer needs more detail.
points: What changes at a larger scale?

posts.hook: After a mock interview, choose one answer to improve.
posts.body:
Read that answer again and ask:

Did I answer the question?
Did I give a specific example?
Did I explain my own contribution?
Could I make the same point more clearly?

Then speak the revised answer aloud. Prep Sarthi reviews your responses and suggests stronger answers from your CV, giving you something concrete to work on. A practice score is feedback, not a hiring prediction.

posts.hook: No percentage improvement to quote? Explain how you checked the work.
posts.body:
An answer can be specific without an invented number.

Describe a test you added, a failure you reproduced, a review you completed or the acceptance criteria you met. State the limits of what you know.

Example, fictional: 'I added tests for missing and duplicate IDs and checked the output against the sample records.'

Practise using evidence from your own work instead of borrowing someone else's results.

posts.hook: Before improving an interview answer, check which question you answered.
posts.body:
If you are asked for a difficult decision, a general project overview may miss the point.

Pause. Identify what the question asks for: an example, a reason, a comparison or a result. Choose one relevant incident. Explain the part that answers the question first, then add context.

Try this in a spoken mock interview where you have to respond to the question you hear.

posts.hook: A suggested interview answer should start with your experience.
posts.body:
Interview Sarthi uses your uploaded resume to suggest answers during an online interview on Windows.

The useful check is simple: can you explain every project, tool and result mentioned? Keep your resume accurate and treat a suggestion as something to review in context.

The app shows the interviewer question and suggested answer on your screen, so you can see what it is responding to.

posts.hook: English question. Hinglish explanation. One interview can use both.
posts.body:
Interview Sarthi supports English, Hindi and Hinglish for live suggested answers on Windows.

It listens to the interviewer and uses your resume as context. The panel stays beside your call app, so the question and suggestion are in one place.

Before relying on a setup, check your audio, language and resume in a test call. Clear product fit matters more than a long feature list.
posts.card_title: Live help in your interview language
points: Check your setup in a test call

posts.hook: Check your interview setup before the call starts.
posts.body:
If you are trying Interview Sarthi, check four things first: the correct resume, the selected audio source, a working Gemini key and an internet connection.

Then open a test call alongside the Windows app. Check that the question is captured and the suggested answer is readable.

The free 30-minute trial lets you evaluate the workflow on your own machine before buying a pass.
posts.card_title: Try the setup on your own Windows PC
points: A test call before the real call

posts.hook: Practising before an interview and getting live assistance are different tasks.
posts.body:
Interview Sarthi is the Windows app for live assistance during the call. It listens to the interviewer and shows suggested answers using your resume.

It works alongside Teams, Zoom, Google Meet and other call apps. You see the question and answer in its panel.

If that is the workflow you need, the product page explains setup and the free trial so you can evaluate it for yourself.
posts.card_title: See how the live Windows app works

posts.hook: What stays on your screen when you share a call? Test your setup.
posts.body:
Interview Sarthi's overlay stays visible to you and is hidden from supported screen sharing on Windows 10 version 2004+ and Windows 11. Capture support varies.

The product page shows a labelled local/shared-view illustration. It is a demonstration of the layout, not a recording of your setup.

Use a test call to check what the other side actually sees before relying on capture exclusion.
posts.card_title: Check the local and shared view
